newsitem.title: KENYA: International community has daunting task on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: International community has daunting task on Zaire.

text.p: The international community has a daunting task in finding a formula to end conflict in Zaire, with even the choice of a suitable venue for talks proving a diplomatic minefield, analysts and diplomats said on Wednesday.

They said peace efforts which were kickstarted by South Africa's President Nelson Mandela in Cape Town last week face a host of problems ranging from deep-rooted mistrust between Zaire and its neighbours to Anglo-French rivalry.
The selection of an acceptable venue for exploratory talks between Zaire's neighbours, who say they want to help, and ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko is proving difficult.
Mandela, Africa's elder statesman, has suggested March 19 talks with Mobutu either in Nairobi, Kenya, or Mobutu's jungle palace at Gbadolite near the border with the Central African Republic.
But both venues present problems.
Key players Rwanda and Uganda are reluctant to travel to Zaire because of accusations they back rebels of Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
"How can we travel to a venue with so much hostility against us? Security and political problems immediately arise for us," a senior Rwandan government official told Reuters by telephone from Kigali.

Nairobi, which has so far hosted two summits on Africa's latest conflict, is being actively opposed by Uganda and Rwanda which both fear Kenya's leadership is too close to Mobutu to maintain impartiality.
This is a view strongly supported by Kabila, who is holding talks with South African officials hoping to broker a ceasefire in the four-month war in Africa's third largest country.

Kabila is an old-time ally of Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni, a former rebel leader who is accused by Zaire and suspected by Kenya of seeking to carve out an empire for the Tutsi tribe in the region.

Kabila was a regular visitor to Uganda in the late 1980s after Museveni took power following a five-year bush war. At the same time exiled Rwandan Tutsis holding senior positions in Museveni's army were fine-tuning plans to invade their homeland.
The invasion finally took place in October 1990 and four years later the Tutsi-dominated army seized power and forced an end to the genocide of up to 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
The link, from Museveni to Rwandan military strongman Paul Kagame to the Banyamulenge Tutsis fighting with Kabila, is at the heart of Tutsi Empire claim.
Meanwhile Pretoria is reluctant to host a full-scale summit on Zaire because of the fear that this could be interpreted as an attempt to upstage Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi.
"It's a dilemma for the South Africans. They have to deal with these complexities before tackling the conflict itself," an African diplomat in Nairobi told Reuters.
The United States and United Nations are keen for a frontline role for the South Africans, who have financial, moral and political muscle.

But concerns are said to be rising in Zaire and among its European allies France and Belgium that Zaire's Anglophone neighbours are upstaging their French-speaking colleagues and tilting the balance in favour of Kabila, who has spent almost all his exile life in English-speaking Tanzania and Uganda.
"We have countered this line of reasoning by inviting and insisting countries like Cameroon, Congo and Togo be fully involved in the regional Zaire peace initiative," said a South African diplomat.
Political analysts say the central role of French-speaking U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun of Algeria was also a factor which should assuage Zairean fears.

Sahnoun, a highly respected diplomat, is currently in South Africa for the secret Kabila talks. The U.N. envoy is seeking an immediate ceasefire in the war, in which Mobutu's ragged army is faring badly.
Kabila's rebels, some of them Zairean Tutsis whose ethnic kin control neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi, took up arms last October and have overrun a strip of east Zaire's borderlands.

Military analysts say the biggest problem in the peace effort will be to persuade Kabila and his rapidly advancing army why they should sue for any peace formula likely to prolong Mobutu's 31-year old rule.
